items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over roughly a five-year period, synthesizing evidence that has informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Key developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a screening and triage tool, and the diversification of decentralised molecular diagnostics through low-complexity automated and manual nucleic acid amplification tests, new near point-of-care platforms, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and strategies like sputum pooling to improve efficiency. Progress in non-sputum specimens including stool, gastric aspirate, and nasopharyngeal samples has improved bacteriological confirmation in children and sputum-scarce populations, while targeted next-generation sequencing is now endorsed for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level. Urine lipoarabinomannan assays offer improved diagnostic yield in people with HIV and advanced disease, and host blood transcriptomic signatures show promise for prognosis and triage, with proteomic, metabolomic, and other biomarker classes advancing through evaluation. Nevertheless, substantial performance, implementation, and equity gaps persist, and no biomarker has yet met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical tuberculosis.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives
items.citation: Zhang D, Cui X, Zhang R et al.. Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives. Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.
items.summary: This review paper examines the current landscape of molecular diagnostic technologies used to detect and characterize pathogens responsible for infectious diseases. The paper surveys nucleic acid amplification approaches, including various forms of polymerase chain reaction optimized for speed, quantification, automation, and point-of-care use, as well as isothermal amplification methods that operate without thermal cycling and are therefore well suited to decentralized testing settings. It also covers CRISPR-based detection systems, which function at constant temperature and are frequently paired with isothermal amplification, and next-generation sequencing, which enables identification of novel pathogens, diagnosis of complex infections, outbreak source tracking, and microbiome analysis relevant to disease susceptibility. The authors conclude that the field is progressing toward integrated hybrid platforms that combine these complementary technologies to overcome the individual limitations of each approach.
items.citation: Takata M, Chikumi H, Yoshifuji A. Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.. Yonago acta medica. 2026

items.title: Molecular Detection of Feline Hemotropic <i>Mycoplasma</i> from Blood Samples of Sick Cats: A Comparative Study Between a Commercial Nucleic Acid Test Card and Conventional Polymerase Chain Reaction.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a rapid commercial nucleic acid test card for detecting feline hemotropic *Mycoplasma* species in clinically ill cats, comparing it against conventional polymerase chain reaction targeting the 16S rRNA gene as the reference standard. Whole blood samples from sick cats presenting to a veterinary teaching hospital in Thailand were tested using both methods. Conventional PCR revealed that '*Candidatus* Mycoplasma haemominutum' was the most frequently detected species, with *Mycoplasma haemofelis* and '*Candidatus* Mycoplasma turicensis' detected at lower frequencies. The commercial nucleic acid test card showed high sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy relative to conventional PCR, delivering results within approximately half an hour, while sequence analysis of discordant samples suggested that low bacterial burdens may account for false-negative results. The authors conclude that this rapid point-of-care assay represents a practical and accurate tool for timely diagnosis of feline hemotropic mycoplasmosis in clinical settings.
items.citation: Nimsuphan B, Ruenphet S, Kengradomkij C et al.. Molecular Detection of Feline Hemotropic <i>Mycoplasma</i> from Blood Samples of Sick Cats: A Comparative Study Between a Commercial Nucleic Acid Test Card and Conventional Polymerase Chain Reaction.. Veterinary sciences. 2026

items.title: Nanomaterials-enabled point-of-care diagnostics for pathogens.
items.summary: This review examines how nanomaterials can enhance point-of-care testing technologies for detecting pathogens, addressing persistent limitations in sensitivity, specificity, multiplexing capability, and quantitative accuracy when working with low-abundance pathogens in complex clinical samples. The authors survey the functional roles of representative nanomaterials across several diagnostic platforms, including lateral flow assays, biosensors, microfluidic systems, and isothermal nucleic acid amplification platforms. Key nanomaterial functions discussed include optical signal output, catalytic signal amplification, target enrichment, and interfacial regulation. The review further organizes nanomaterial-assisted recognition mechanisms into three categories—pathogen surface recognition, reactive oxygen species-mediated signal conversion, and nucleic acid recognition—and considers their application across respiratory, urinary, and fecal specimen types. The authors conclude that these advances collectively support the development of more sensitive, integrated, and field-deployable diagnostic tools for infectious disease control.
items.citation: Wu J, Wang D, Ye W et al.. Nanomaterials-enabled point-of-care diagnostics for pathogens.. Frontiers in medicine. 2026

items.title: Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.
items.summary: This paper describes the development of a centrifugal microfluidic platform called mFIND, designed to simultaneously detect multiple respiratory pathogens including influenza A and B, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV. The system integrates lyophilized reagents into four independent reaction chambers on a chip, paired with a portable analyzer that automates sample handling, isothermal amplification, and real-time fluorescence detection within fifteen minutes using very small reaction volumes. The platform demonstrated extremely low limits of detection for all four target pathogens and showed no cross-reactivity against a broad panel of non-target organisms. Clinical validation using a substantial set of positive patient samples confirmed complete agreement with standard quantitative PCR results. The authors conclude that mFIND offers a practical point-of-care nucleic acid testing solution suitable for decentralized settings, combining rapid turnaround, simplified operation, and parallel multiplex detection.
items.citation: He P, Feng Y, Zhou X et al.. Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.. Biosensors & bioelectronics. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical translation. The authors surveyed how genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic approaches, combined with deep learning architectures, can decode complex biological datasets to reveal disease mechanisms and molecular targets. They analyzed applications across the drug development pipeline, including target deconvolution, drug repositioning, de novo compound discovery, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment, with illustrative cases drawn from oncology, neurodegenerative diseases, and cardiovascular conditions. The review finds that this convergence accelerates target identification and lead optimization while enabling more precise clinical trial design, though challenges remain around harmonizing disparate data streams, ensuring reproducibility, and reducing algorithmic bias. The authors conclude that combining multiomics with artificial intelligence opens new avenues for data-driven therapeutic innovation and marks a significant advance in bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Loss-of-function mutation in Omicron variants reduces spike protein expression and attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection
items.citation: Michelle N. Vu, R. Elias Alvarado, Dorothea R. Morris et al.. Loss-of-function mutation in Omicron variants reduces spike protein expression and attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection. Nature Communications. 2026

items.title: mRNA vaccine immunity is enhanced by hepatocyte detargeting and not dependent on dendritic cell expression
items.summary: This study investigated how cell-type-specific expression of mRNA vaccine-encoded proteins influences immune responses, addressing a gap in understanding since lipid nanoparticle-delivered mRNA can transfect diverse cell types. Using synthetic microRNA target sites incorporated into mRNA constructs, the researchers selectively silenced vaccine expression in professional antigen-presenting cells, hepatocytes, or myocytes in mouse models. They found that expression in professional antigen-presenting cells was dispensable for priming antigen-specific T cells, while myocyte expression drove similar or stronger immune responses, suggesting cross-presentation or cross-dressing mechanisms are more important than direct antigen presentation. Hepatocyte expression, by contrast, suppressed T cell responses partly through the PD1/PDL1 axis, and silencing expression specifically in hepatocytes enhanced anti-tumor immunity and reduced tumor burden in a lymphoma model. These findings demonstrate that non-antigen-presenting cell expression critically shapes mRNA vaccine immunogenicity, and that microRNA target site engineering represents a strategy to boost or modulate vaccine-induced immunity.
items.citation: Adam R. Marks, Sophia Siu, Filippo Bianchini et al.. mRNA vaccine immunity is enhanced by hepatocyte detargeting and not dependent on dendritic cell expression. Nature Biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective
items.summary: This paper examines the regulatory landscape governing cell-derived extracellular vesicles as therapeutic and diagnostic products, with particular attention to inconsistencies across major jurisdictions. The authors analyze how existing medicinal product frameworks in the European Union, the United States, Japan, and other regions classify and oversee EV-based products, noting that their acellular nature creates uneven mapping onto established regulatory categories such as biologics and advanced therapy medicinal products. A central finding is that regulatory heterogeneity generates significant challenges around product classification, quality attributes, potency assessment, and comparability across clinical development programs. The authors argue that EV-based products can and should be developed within existing medicinal product frameworks, provided that regulatory tools are applied consistently and that poorly defined areas such as classification criteria and critical quality attributes are clarified through ongoing dialogue. The review is positioned as a synthesis intended to inform regulatory agencies, harmonization bodies, and scientific societies working toward safe and internationally credible clinical translation of EV-based therapies.
items.citation: Tania Limongi, Paola Milla, Barbara Stella et al.. Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective. Journal of Extracellular Vesicles. 2026

items.title: Dairy cows infected with influenza A(H5N1) reveals low infectious dose and transmission barriers
items.citation: Carolyn M. Lee, Natalie N. Tarbuck, Hannah J. Cochran et al.. Dairy cows infected with influenza A(H5N1) reveals low infectious dose and transmission barriers. Nature Communications. 2026

items.title: Evolutionary characterization of lung cancer metastasis
items.summary: This study investigated how lung cancer evolves and spreads from the primary tumor through to metastatic disease across the full course of illness in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Using hundreds of longitudinally collected primary and metastatic tumor samples drawn from patients enrolled in two prospective studies, the researchers performed DNA sequencing to reconstruct the evolutionary trajectories of tumors from diagnosis to death. They found that metastatic genomes diverge substantially from their ancestral primary tumors, acquiring additional driver alterations and genome doubling events after dissemination, and that multiple distinct primary tumor subclones contributed independently to metastatic seeding in the majority of patients. More than half of all metastases were themselves seeded by other metastases rather than directly by the primary tumor, with the duration a metastasis existed influencing its likelihood of onward spread, and most metastatic migrations occurring within the same anatomical cavity. The small subset of subclones that spread beyond the thorax disseminated widely and were enriched for copy-number alterations, suggesting chromosomal instability as a potential driver of extrathoracic spread and highlighting that single-biopsy approaches substantially underestimate metastatic diversity in advanced disease.
items.citation: Sonya Hessey, Abigail Bunkum, Ariana Huebner et al.. Evolutionary characterization of lung cancer metastasis. Nature. 2026

items.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
items.summary: This paper investigated whether language models can navigate large document networks by using the Wikipedia Game — a task where players must reach a target article by following only hyperlinks — as a benchmark for information retrieval. The researchers compared sentence embedding models and large language models across multiple Wikipedia language editions and academic literature datasets, constructing large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and paper citations to enable evaluation without dependence on third-party APIs. Models were benchmarked against human players and a term-frequency baseline across diverse languages and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, though several frontier reasoning and instruction-tuned models achieved comparable success rates. Performance varied considerably across languages and subject domains, with implications for practitioners deploying these models in real-world information retrieval contexts.
items.citation: Alexander Hickey, Joanna Knight, James Bishop. Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
items.summary: The paper investigates whether machines can perform visual non-verbal reasoning, a domain where even advanced AI systems struggle with tasks such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions of interest, partly because the intermediate steps in visual reasoning are implicit and difficult to verify. To address this, the authors introduce GenVerOpt, a framework that integrates generation, verification, and optimisation into a unified pipeline, enabling iterative refinement of candidate solutions on a per-sample basis rather than relying solely on patterns learned during training. This approach is designed to mirror human problem-solving, where multiple possibilities are considered and evaluated until a satisfactory solution emerges. Tested across diverse domains, GenVerOpt surpasses human performance on abstract IQ puzzles, matches clinical experts in prostate cancer segmentation, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in liver vessel reconstruction and tumour boundary alignment. The authors conclude that machine reasoning can be meaningfully extended beyond language into the visual domain, positioning non-verbal reasoning as a key foundation for more generalizable artificial intelligence.
items.citation: Shaheer U. Saeed, Zion Tse, Gregory Slabaugh et al.. Can machines reason non-verbally?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
items.summary: This paper investigates recursive self-improvement (RSI), the process by which an AI system converts interaction experience into lasting performance gains without incurring prohibitive external feedback costs. The authors introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on predictive world models that guide both action selection and the curation of learning data, with compatibility checks determining whether updated policy-model pairs are retained. The framework was evaluated across a range of computational and scientific tasks, including code repair, graphical user interface navigation, laboratory planning, and chemical reaction optimization. Across all domains, RSI-Anything substantially outperformed baseline approaches, with iterative policy updates more than doubling laboratory-planning scores over successive versions and achieving markedly higher reaction yields than Bayesian optimization under the same experimental budget. The results support the claim that predictive world models, combined with principled retention of system updates, enable robust recursive improvement across diverse and heterogeneous environments.
items.citation: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu et al.. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models. arXiv. 2026

items.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
items.summary: Vision-Language Models are increasingly deployed for tasks requiring spatial and relational reasoning about images, but whether their internal representations reliably encode such structured information remains uncertain. This paper introduces a new metric called EICS to measure whether representations consistently encode specific concepts under controlled interventions, alongside a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from scene graphs. Testing across multiple VLM architectures, the authors find that spatial relations are encoded far less faithfully in internal representations than lexical information, even in models that perform well above chance on standard compositional benchmarks. Further probing reveals that while relational information is detectable at the tokens corresponding to the predicate itself, it is systematically lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation through end-of-sequence tokens or mean pooling. The study exposes a fundamental failure mode invisible to output-based evaluation: relational information present in the model's input is not preserved in the downstream representations the model actually uses.
items.citation: Shubh Garg, Chen Shani. When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
items.summary: This paper investigates the choice of objective functions for deep learning regression on tabular data, an area that has received comparatively little systematic study despite growing interest in tabular deep learning. The authors conducted a broad empirical re-evaluation of multiple proposed regression objectives across a diverse collection of tabular datasets and several neural network backbones, using consistent evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison. They found that many alternative objectives offer limited or inconsistent benefits over a well-tuned Mean Squared Error baseline, but that quantile loss provides reliable aggregate improvements across backbones. The study further identifies a previously underappreciated limitation: different regions of the input space with varying levels of target noise reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs, meaning a single global early-stopping criterion forces a suboptimal compromise across uncertainty regions. To address this, the authors propose a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that incorporates input-dependent label smoothing, which improves performance over standard quantile loss on several backbones.
items.citation: Danil Rudenko, Georgii Bulgakov, Nikolay Kartashev et al.. Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping. arXiv. 2026

items.title: How Social Reinforcement Shapes Word-of-Mouth: A Conviction-Based Model for Marketing Diffusion and Network Targeting
items.summary: This paper examines how social reinforcement during product adoption shapes the strength with which consumers subsequently advocate for that product, a mechanism largely ignored by classical diffusion models. The authors introduce the Pressure Threshold model, a conviction-based diffusion framework in which an individual's influence on others grows with the cumulative social pressure they experienced at the time of their own adoption. They analyze the marketing implications of this mechanism, demonstrating that it fundamentally shifts optimal network targeting strategies toward consumers situated in dense, cohesive network regions where repeated social exposure can amplify downstream word-of-mouth. Despite the added complexity this introduces into optimization, scalable heuristics with data-dependent performance guarantees remain effective, and simulations across synthetic and real-world networks show that accounting for reinforcement substantially improves the impact of seeding interventions in clustered environments. Validation against time-stamped social media cascades further shows that the model outperforms standard diffusion approaches in predictive accuracy, supporting the empirical relevance of conviction-driven amplification.
items.citation: Abhishek K. Umrawal, Curt Stutsman, Camille Woods et al.. How Social Reinforcement Shapes Word-of-Mouth: A Conviction-Based Model for Marketing Diffusion and Network Targeting. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a point-of-care rapid antigen test, the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit, for detecting respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus in children presenting to a pediatric emergency department with acute respiratory symptoms. In a prospective design, nasopharyngeal swabs from children aged eighteen years and under were tested using both the rapid kit and multiplex real-time PCR, which served as the reference standard. The rapid test demonstrated very high sensitivity and specificity for both pathogens, with excellent agreement with PCR results for adenovirus and RSV alike. RSV positivity was most common in infants under one year of age, while adenovirus positivity peaked in school-aged children, and distinct clinical predictors were identified for each pathogen. The authors conclude that this dual-pathogen rapid test offers clinically useful diagnostic performance and may support timely decision-making in pediatric emergency care settings.
items.citation: Ates B, Kacar A, Kok S et al.. Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples. 2026

items.title: Point prevalence assessments of five respiratory viruses in adults ≥ 50 years of age in Germany by multi-pathogen rapid antigen testing on June 1, 2024, and December 15, 2024.
items.summary: This study investigated the circulation of five respiratory viruses among community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older in Germany using two point prevalence assessments conducted in summer and winter. Participants performed multi-pathogen rapid antigen self-tests capable of detecting adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus, and reported symptoms, healthcare use, work absenteeism, and other relevant factors. The overall pathogen detection rate was low, with the majority of tests returning negative results, but adenovirus was the most frequently detected pathogen in both assessment rounds, a finding considered underrepresented in routine surveillance. SARS-CoV-2 was associated with the greatest clinical and economic burden, driving the highest rates of healthcare consultations and work absenteeism among positive cases. The authors conclude that community-based point prevalence screening can uncover asymptomatic reservoirs and underreported viral circulation that conventional surveillance may miss.
items.citation: Anggitakirana M, Nacov JA, Salmanton-García J et al.. Point prevalence assessments of five respiratory viruses in adults ≥ 50 years of age in Germany by multi-pathogen rapid antigen testing on June 1, 2024, and December 15, 2024.. Infection. 2026

items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate article addresses a central question in exercise immunology: whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection. The authors review evidence showing that moderate, short-duration exercise generally benefits immune defense, particularly in older adults and those with chronic disease, while high-performance athletes and military personnel appear to experience elevated infection burdens. The debate examines whether arduous exercise independently causes immune suppression or whether confounding factors such as sleep disruption, nutritional deficits, psychological stress, travel, and environmental extremes are primarily responsible. Contested issues include whether athletes are genuinely more infection-prone than the general population, the validity of biomarkers used to assess immune health under heavy training loads, and the overall quality of evidence underpinning claims about exercise-induced immunosuppression. Both sides agree that infection susceptibility is multifactorial, but the question of whether exercise per se is a causative factor of increased infection risk in athletes remains unresolved, with the authors calling for more rigorous empirical research.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process
items.summary: This paper describes the development and goals of the Rome V criteria for disorders of gut–brain interaction, a class of gastrointestinal conditions driven by combinations of motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, altered gut microbiota, and changes in central nervous system processing. The Rome V process involved a comprehensive review of evidence accumulated since the previous Rome IV iteration, with the aim of refining diagnostic criteria and clinical management frameworks. Key updates include revised definitions of these disorders, expanded coverage of dietary, microbial, pharmacogenomic, biopsychosocial, gender, and cross-cultural factors, as well as updated diagnostic algorithms and therapeutic approaches. The process also prioritized incorporating patient illness experiences and sociocultural perspectives while reducing the use of imprecise or stigmatizing terminology. Overall, the paper presents Rome V as an evidence-based evolution of the field's foundational diagnostic and management framework for gut–brain interaction disorders.
items.citation: Douglas A. Drossman, L Chang, Jan F. Tack. Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process. Gastroenterology. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with a particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search to gather existing evidence on exercise immunology across patient, recreationally active, and athlete populations with spinal cord injury. They explored how autonomic dysfunction and altered catecholamine concentrations following injury, especially in individuals with tetraplegia, may directly depress immunity through effects on lymphocytes and adrenergic receptor signaling, while also considering contributions from altered muscular, endocrine, and cardiovascular function. The review found that although spinal cord injury broadly suppresses immune function, some immune responses to exercise — such as natural killer cell cytotoxicity increases and mucosal immunity changes in tetraplegia — appear preserved or similar to those seen in able-bodied individuals, suggesting compensatory mechanisms such as sympathetic reflex activity or receptor hypersensitivity may offset some deficits. The authors conclude that exercise and rehabilitation can improve certain immune and autonomic measures following spinal cord injury, and call for further research to clarify the mechanisms involved and their implications for infection susceptibility.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria Louise Goosey-Tolfrey, NICOLETTE CLAIRE BISHOP. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper examined graft-versus-host disease, a potentially multi-systemic complication arising from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in which donor lymphocytes attack host tissues, with particular focus on its chronic form and associated physical impairments. The authors reviewed the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease alongside available evidence from both animal and human studies on the effects of exercise as an adjunct therapy in affected patients. Their findings suggest that exercise training holds promise for improving physical fitness and possibly immune function while reducing fatigue in this population. However, the authors conclude that the evidence base remains insufficient, calling for more randomized controlled trials that specifically target patients with graft-versus-host disease rather than broader transplant populations.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses

items.title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress in disease pathogenesis: its implications for therapy
items.summary: This review paper examines the role of endoplasmic reticulum stress and the unfolded protein response in the development and progression of a broad spectrum of diseases. The authors systematically synthesize current knowledge on the three main UPR signaling branches and their regulatory mechanisms, detailing how these pathways govern protein homeostasis, stress adaptation, and apoptosis. The review explores how dysregulated or prolonged ER stress contributes to conditions including cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic diseases, and autoimmune conditions, through mechanisms such as inflammation, aberrant protein accumulation, and impaired immune signaling. In the context of cancer specifically, the authors highlight how ER stress reshapes the tumor microenvironment and facilitates immune evasion, complicating treatment. The paper concludes that therapeutically targeting ER stress pathways holds considerable promise for restoring cellular homeostasis and improving clinical outcomes across multiple disease contexts.
items.citation: Siyu Wei, Nan Zhang, Hao Zhang et al.. Endoplasmic reticulum stress in disease pathogenesis: its implications for therapy. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
items.summary: This paper investigated whether language models can effectively navigate large document networks by testing them on the Wikipedia Game, where players must traverse from one article to another using only hyperlinks. The researchers evaluated sentence embedding models and large language models across five Wikipedia language editions and five academic literature datasets, constructing large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and paper citations to enable testing without reliance on external APIs. Models were benchmarked against human players and a TF-IDF baseline to assess their relative navigation capabilities. No model significantly outperformed humans, though the top-performing models achieved comparable success rates, and performance rankings varied meaningfully across languages and subject domains. The findings have practical implications for deploying language models in information retrieval tasks that require traversing large, domain-specific document collections.
items.citation: Alexander Hickey, Joanna Knight, James Bishop. Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
items.summary: The paper investigates why modern AI systems struggle with visual non-verbal reasoning tasks, such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions of interest, even though they perform well on verbal and logical reasoning. The authors argue that visual reasoning is fundamentally harder to model because its intermediate steps are implicit and lack clear verification methods, unlike language-based reasoning. To address this, they introduce GenVerOpt, a framework that unifies generation, verification, and iterative optimisation into a unified reasoning pipeline, allowing models to refine solutions on a per-sample basis rather than relying solely on patterns learned during training. Tested across diverse domains, the framework surpasses human performance on abstract IQ puzzles, matches clinicians in prostate cancer segmentation, and outperforms experts in liver vessel reconstruction and tumour boundary delineation. The authors conclude that machine reasoning can be meaningfully extended beyond language into the visual domain, offering a foundation for more flexible and generalisable intelligence.
items.citation: Shaheer U. Saeed, Zion Tse, Gregory Slabaugh et al.. Can machines reason non-verbally?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
items.summary: This paper presents DyssomniaNN, a computational framework designed to model human sleep disorders and the disconnect between objective sleep duration and subjective feelings of restedness. The framework integrates established regulatory models of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with a hypothalamic flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic spiking neural network to simulate sleep–wake dynamics across five clinical cohorts, including healthy controls and patients with delayed-phase circadian disorder, chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. Synthetic neural activity generated by the model was validated against empirical human electroencephalography data, showing close convergence across canonical frequency bands. A novel metric called the Well-Rested Index was introduced to quantify restorative sleep quality, and simulations demonstrated that total sleep time alone does not predict recovery—paradoxical insomnia produced normal sleep duration but poor restoration due to persistent cortical beta-band activity, while narcolepsy generated severe nocturnal fragmentation despite sleep occurring. The authors propose DyssomniaNN as an in silico platform for investigating sleep disorder mechanisms and testing virtual pharmacological interventions.
items.citation: Daniel Szelogowski. DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness. arXiv. 2026

items.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of recursive self-improvement in AI systems, where agents must convert interaction experience into lasting performance gains without relying excessively on costly external feedback. The authors developed RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on predictive world models that guides both action selection and learning-data curation, while using compatibility checks to determine which updated policy-model pairs should be retained. The framework was evaluated across a range of computational and scientific tasks, including code repair, graphical user interface navigation, laboratory planning, and chemical reaction optimization. Across all domains, RSI-Anything demonstrated consistent improvements over baselines, including surpassing Bayesian optimization in reaction yield under equivalent experimental budgets and more than doubling laboratory-planning scores across successive policy versions. The results support the claim that combining predictive world models with principled retention of system updates enables robust recursive self-improvement across diverse and heterogeneous environments.
items.citation: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu et al.. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models. arXiv. 2026

items.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
items.summary: Vision-Language Models are widely used for image reasoning, but this paper investigates whether their internal representations actually encode structured spatial relationships faithfully. The researchers developed a new metric called EICS to assess whether concepts remain stably represented under controlled single-concept changes, and paired it with a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from scene graphs. Testing across multiple VLM architectures, they found that spatial relations are encoded far less faithfully in internal representations than lexical information, even when the same models perform well above chance on standard compositional benchmarks. Further probing revealed that while relational information is detectable at the tokens corresponding to individual predicates, it is lost when the representation is aggregated into a global form via end-of-sequence tokens or mean pooling. This exposes a systematic failure that output-based evaluations cannot detect: the relational information present in a model's input is not preserved in the downstream representations the model actually uses.
items.citation: Shubh Garg, Chen Shani. When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
items.summary: This paper investigates the choice of objective functions for deep learning regression on tabular data, an area that has received less systematic attention than model architecture design. The authors conducted a broad empirical re-evaluation of multiple proposed regression objectives across a diverse collection of tabular datasets and several neural network backbones, using consistent evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison. They found that most alternative objectives offer limited or inconsistent improvements over a well-tuned Mean Squared Error baseline, though quantile loss emerged as a consistently beneficial alternative across backbones. The authors further identified a fundamental limitation of global early stopping: regions of the input space with different levels of target noise tend to reach their optimal predictive performance at different training epochs, creating an unavoidable compromise when a single checkpoint is selected. To address this, they proposed a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that incorporates input-dependent label smoothing, which improves performance over standard quantile loss on several backbones.
items.citation: Danil Rudenko, Georgii Bulgakov, Nikolay Kartashev et al.. Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis Detection with MiniDock MTB Using Swab Samples
items.summary: This prospective, cross-sectional study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of MiniDock MTB, a novel tuberculosis detection test designed for use in peripheral health settings, across multiple countries including India, Nigeria, the Philippines, South Africa, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia. Participants aged twelve years and older with presumptive pulmonary tuberculosis were tested using both sputum swabs and tongue swabs, with results benchmarked against sputum culture, smear microscopy, and the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay. MiniDock MTB demonstrated sensitivity exceeding eighty-five percent with sputum and nearly eighty percent with tongue swabs, with specificity above ninety-seven percent for both sample types, closely matching the performance of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra while substantially outperforming smear microscopy. The test met World Health Organization accuracy targets for near-point-of-care tuberculosis diagnostics for both sputum and nonsputum samples and received good usability ratings from healthcare workers. These findings support MiniDock MTB as a promising diagnostic tool capable of improving tuberculosis case detection in diverse clinical settings where advanced laboratory infrastructure may be limited.
items.citation: Seda Yerlikaya, Masuzyo Chirwa, Bukola Ajide et al.. Pulmonary Tuberculosis Detection with MiniDock MTB Using Swab Samples. New England Journal of Medicine. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This review examines advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over roughly a five-year period, synthesizing the scientific evidence that has informed updated World Health Organization policy guidance. The work consolidates recommendations for tuberculosis detection and drug-resistance testing across populations, specimen types, and care settings, integrating screening, diagnosis, and resistance testing into a unified framework. Key developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a frontline screening tool, the diversification of decentralised molecular diagnostics through multiple rapid nucleic acid amplification test platforms, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and programmatic strategies like sputum pooling to reach sputum-scarce populations including children. Targeted next-generation sequencing has been recognized as an endorsed approach for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing, while urine lipoarabinomannan assays offer diagnostic benefit in people with HIV and advanced disease despite performance limitations. The review concludes that although host transcriptomic and other biomarkers show promising prognostic and triage performance, no biomarker has yet met criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical tuberculosis, highlighting persistent performance, implementation, and equity gaps.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Smart electroactive molecularly imprinted polymers (e-MIPs) for precision diagnostics and point-of-care technologies: Design, mechanisms, and clinical translation.
items.summary: This review examines smart electroactive molecularly imprinted polymers, a class of synthetic materials that combine selective molecular recognition with electrochemical signal transduction as alternatives to biological recognition elements like antibodies and enzymes. The authors critically evaluate recent advances in the design and synthesis of these materials, including the roles of functional monomers, electropolymerization techniques, nanostructuring, and conductive nanomaterials in governing analytical performance and electron-transfer behavior. The review surveys their application across a range of diagnostic contexts, including infectious disease detection, disease-biomarker sensing, wearable systems, and point-of-care technologies, supported by representative case studies demonstrating rapid, label-free analysis of real biological samples. The authors also address persistent challenges such as binding-site heterogeneity, nonspecific adsorption, reproducibility, scalability, and the need for rigorous clinical validation before widespread deployment. Overall, the review positions these materials as promising candidates for next-generation precision diagnostics while outlining the scientific and translational hurdles that remain to be overcome.
items.venue: Advances in colloid and interface science

items.title: Predicted Preferences for Tuberculosis Point-of-Care Tests Among Tuberculosis-Affected Individuals in 5 High Burden Countries.
items.summary: This paper investigated how individuals affected by tuberculosis value point-of-care diagnostic tests relative to standard facility-based testing across multiple high-burden countries. Using discrete choice experiment data from a large multinational sample of tuberculosis-affected participants, the researchers simulated preferences for different test characteristics. They found that point-of-care tuberculosis tests were strongly preferred by affected individuals, and this preference held even when point-of-care options were modeled with somewhat lower diagnostic accuracy than conventional testing approaches. The findings suggest that convenience and accessibility factors may outweigh accuracy trade-offs in the preferences of those most affected by tuberculosis.

items.title: Rapid Diagnostics for Distinguishing Bacterial and Viral Infections: A Review of Technologies, Clinical Utility, and Stewardship Implications.
items.summary: This review examines the challenge of distinguishing bacterial from viral infections at the point of care, a diagnostic uncertainty that drives inappropriate antibiotic prescribing and contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The authors surveyed a broad range of current and emerging rapid diagnostic technologies, including molecular assays, rapid antigen tests, biomarker-based platforms, host-response systems, hematologic methods, and artificial intelligence decision-support tools. Each technology was evaluated against criteria including diagnostic accuracy, turnaround time, cost, accessibility, and practical clinical actionability. While some point-of-care technologies can return results within minutes, the review finds that their ability to consistently fit the workflow and decision-making demands of outpatient and emergency settings remains variable and incompletely established. The authors conclude that future advances in antimicrobial stewardship will require rapid diagnostic systems that integrate seamlessly into frontline care to meaningfully reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.
items.citation: Javanmard M, Vellanki R, Fardoost A et al.. Rapid Diagnostics for Distinguishing Bacterial and Viral Infections: A Review of Technologies, Clinical Utility, and Stewardship Implications.. Biosensors. 2026

items.title: Gut microbiome and metabolic health: mechanisms and precision interventions
items.summary: This review examines the gut microbiome as a central regulator of metabolic health, exploring how microbial communities influence energy balance, insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and inter-organ communication through metabolites and signaling pathways. The authors synthesize mechanistic evidence spanning short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acid signaling, gut barrier integrity, immune modulation, and the microbiota-gut-brain-pancreas axis, while also cataloguing disease-associated microbial alterations in obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and metabolic syndrome. Evidence from germ-free models, fecal microbiota transplantation, and strain-level interventions is assessed to support a causal role for microbial ecology in shaping metabolic outcomes. The review critically evaluates therapeutic strategies including probiotics, prebiotics, dietary modulation, and fecal microbiota transplantation, and discusses how multi-omics technologies, metabolic modeling, and machine learning can advance precision approaches. To organize these insights, the authors propose a precision microbiome intervention pipeline and a conceptual framework called the Precision Microbiome Intervention Triangle to explain inter-individual variability in responses to microbiome-targeted therapies.
items.citation: Zhengrui Li, Sudeshna Samui, J S Liu et al.. Gut microbiome and metabolic health: mechanisms and precision interventions. Gut Microbes. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and translational medicine. The authors synthesize current multiomics approaches — including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic profiling — alongside advanced AI methodologies such as deep learning to analyze how these tools collectively illuminate disease mechanisms at the molecular level. The review covers the application of these combined approaches across the full drug development pipeline, including target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound design, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Disease areas including oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular conditions are used as illustrative cases, while persistent challenges such as data harmonization, reproducibility, and algorithmic bias are also addressed. The authors conclude that the convergence of multiomics and AI offers transformative potential for hypothesis generation, data-driven therapeutic discovery, and more precise clinical interventions, heralding a new era in bench-to-clinic medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: A comprehensive survey of AI agents in healthcare
items.summary: This survey systematically examines the landscape of AI agents applied to healthcare, focusing on how general-purpose agentic frameworks characterized by autonomy, planning, and tool use must be adapted to the safety-critical demands of medical decision-making. The authors reviewed a large body of recent studies drawn from major academic databases and developed a taxonomic framework organized around three pillars: the perception of multimodal clinical data such as electronic health records, imaging, and genomics; core agent capabilities including reasoning, memory, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration; and an application ecosystem structured by stakeholder roles spanning clinicians, patients, researchers, and administrators. The review finds that the field has grown exponentially and provides analysis of evaluation frameworks alongside an assessment of deployment readiness across technical, evidentiary, and governance dimensions. Despite this rapid growth, the authors conclude that current research remains largely confined to benchmark and controlled evaluation settings, and that translating AI agents into genuine clinical practice will require substantial advances in reliability, privacy protection, governance, and operational integration.
items.citation: Gelei Xu, Xueyang Li, Yixiong Chen et al.. A comprehensive survey of AI agents in healthcare. Journal of Biomedical Informatics. 2026

items.title: A Comprehensive JWST Slitless Spectroscopic Census of $\sim$12,000 Emission-Line Galaxies at Redshift $0\sim9$ in COSMOS
items.summary: This paper presents a large-scale spectroscopic survey of emission-line galaxies using JWST's near-infrared slitless spectroscopy mode, aimed at characterizing star formation, chemical enrichment, and AGN activity across a wide range of cosmic epochs. The study leveraged wide-field slitless spectroscopy from the COSMOS-3D program, covering a contiguous area in the COSMOS field and combining grism spectroscopy with deep multi-band imaging to build a homogeneous sample spanning redshifts from zero to nine. To overcome the source confusion problem inherent to slitless spectroscopy, the authors developed a multi-step identification framework incorporating convolutional neural networks and large language models to emulate and streamline the human identification process. The resulting catalog contains over twelve thousand objects with spectroscopic redshifts, emission-line measurements, and derived physical properties, detecting a broad suite of emission lines that enable a continuous census of galaxies across cosmic time. Composite spectra constructed in multiple redshift bins also revealed faint features — including higher-order hydrogen recombination lines, CO absorption bands, and iron emission lines — that are undetectable in individual spectra, demonstrating the power of this approach for building large, unbiased spectroscopic samples.
items.citation: Shuqi Fu, Zijian Zhang, Danyang Jiang et al.. A Comprehensive JWST Slitless Spectroscopic Census of $\sim$12,000 Emission-Line Galaxies at Redshift $0\sim9$ in COSMOS. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Where to Look Matters: Rethinking Sub-Volume Sampling in 3D Medical Self-supervised Learning
items.summary: This paper investigates a fundamental but overlooked component of self-supervised learning for three-dimensional medical images: how sub-volumes are sampled during pretraining. The authors demonstrate through controlled experiments that the quality of cropped sub-volumes directly impacts downstream task performance, framing sub-volume sampling as a "where-to-look" problem rather than a random process. They propose a plug-and-play framework called a coarse-to-fine probe bank that selects training crops guided by three principles—anatomy-awareness, informativeness, and diversity—instantiated in both a lightweight variant using geometric and image-statistical cues and a richer variant leveraging frozen visual features. Across multiple self-supervised learning backbones and downstream medical imaging tasks, the lightweight variant consistently outperforms random cropping baselines. Mechanistic analyses reveal that the improvements stem from more anatomically meaningful and informative observations, reduced spatial redundancy, more efficient learning dynamics, and better-structured learned representations.
items.citation: Junkai Liu, Le Zhang. Where to Look Matters: Rethinking Sub-Volume Sampling in 3D Medical Self-supervised Learning. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Monodromy of Tate-Linear varieties
items.summary: The paper addresses a question in arithmetic geometry concerning the structure of special subvarieties within the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties in characteristic p. Specifically, it studies Tate-linear subvarieties of central leaves of this moduli space over the algebraic closure of a finite field. The authors prove a rigidity result: if a smooth subvariety of a central leaf is Tate-linear at a single point, then it is necessarily Tate-linear at every point. This is established through a careful analysis of the p-adic monodromy groups associated to Tate-linear varieties, building on recent foundational work in the field.
items.citation: Livia Grammatica. Monodromy of Tate-Linear varieties. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of building surrogate models for computationally expensive implosion simulations, where physical diagnostic quantities recorded during simulation can organize sharply varying responses but are unavailable at prediction time without running additional calculations. The authors developed a Gaussian process surrogate framework that learns these physical-state diagnostics from design variables alone, using cross-fitted state estimates to augment the design representation and optionally incorporating a soft mixture-of-experts approach targeting different response bands. Testing on a large database of paired one-dimensional implosion simulations, the learned physical-state supervision substantially reduced mean squared log-response error for both random holdout and design-space extrapolation compared to baselines, with control experiments using random projections and shuffled states confirming that the gains are specific to physically meaningful supervision. The mixture-of-experts component proved beneficial at smaller training set sizes but offered little additional advantage at larger budgets, and results on a second material system revealed weaker extrapolation gains and cases where expert specialization degraded accuracy. The authors conclude that physical-state supervision is a broadly useful representation strategy for finite-data surrogates, while expert specialization requires validation to determine whether it is appropriate for a given problem.
items.citation: Chang Liu, Hao Shen, Chuanying Li. Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Shared Canonical Component Removal Beyond Expert Views
items.summary: This paper investigates what predictive information black-box models trained on raw inputs capture beyond what clinically derived expert features contain. The authors developed an audit framework called Shared Canonical Component Removal (SCCR), which selectively removes directions that are strongly shared between learned raw and expert embeddings, distinguishing it from standard residualization or concept erasure approaches. The framework was evaluated on synthetic data and three clinical tasks spanning coronary artery disease detection, antidepressant treatment dropout prediction, and skin lesion classification. SCCR was found to identify the limitations of expert views and recover residual predictive signal in the raw model while minimizing redundancy with expert-derived representations, thereby clarifying the nature and origin of the performance gap between raw and expert-feature-based models.
items.citation: Jose Roberto Tello Ayala, Akl C. Fahed, Roy Perlis et al.. Shared Canonical Component Removal Beyond Expert Views. arXiv. 2026

items.title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
items.summary: This paper investigates whether large language models can generate reliable unit tests for quantum software, a task complicated by the probabilistic nature of quantum programs, numerical tolerances, and domain-specific correctness criteria. The authors developed QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites by comparing their verdicts against independent benchmark checkers rather than treating the generated tests themselves as ground truth. The framework prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and assesses test quality across multiple validation cohorts on challenges spanning two quantum programming frameworks. Testing five models across these tasks revealed that while generated test suites almost always execute successfully, their ability to discriminate between correct and faulty implementations is substantially weaker, with the best-performing model reaching notably lower quality scores on one framework than the other, demonstrating that executability alone overstates true test quality. The work also introduces oracle-verified synthetic mutants to stabilize bug-detection estimates when naturally occurring faulty solutions are scarce, and presents QTestBench as a reproducible benchmark for assessing the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
items.citation: Meriem Terki, Nouhaila Innan, Minghao Shao et al.. QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This review examines progress in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research from 2020 to 2025, synthesizing advances that have informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance. Digital chest radiography supported by computer-aided detection has been established as a core screening and triage tool, while decentralised molecular diagnosis has expanded through multiple classes of rapid nucleic acid amplification tests, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and workflow innovations including sputum pooling. Molecular diagnostics have improved bacteriological confirmation in children and sputum-scarce populations through expanded use across non-sputum specimens, and targeted next-generation sequencing is now recognised for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level. Urine lipoarabinomannan assays improve diagnostic yield in people with HIV with advanced disease, and host blood transcriptomic signatures show strong prognostic and triage performance, with proteomic, metabolomic, and other biomarker classes advancing through clinical evaluation. Despite these advances, significant performance, implementation, and equity gaps persist, and no biomarker has yet met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical tuberculosis.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.
items.summary: This review examines the current landscape of molecular diagnostic technologies applied to infectious disease detection and pathogen characterization. The paper covers two principal approaches: nucleic acid amplification methods, including polymerase chain reaction variants and isothermal amplification techniques, and next-generation sequencing for comprehensive genomic analysis. Key developments in polymerase chain reaction include advances toward faster reaction times, quantification capabilities, full automation, and point-of-care deployment, while isothermal amplification methods offer the advantage of constant-temperature operation without thermal cycling equipment, making them particularly suitable for decentralized testing. CRISPR-based detection systems, which function at constant temperature and are often paired with isothermal amplification, are highlighted as an emerging diagnostic approach. The review concludes that next-generation sequencing adds value beyond pathogen detection by enabling outbreak source tracking, monitoring of pathogen evolution, and microbiome analysis, and anticipates that future molecular diagnostics will progress through integration of these diverse technologies into hybrid platforms.
items.citation: Takata M, Chikumi H, Yoshifuji A. Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.. Yonago acta medica. 2026

items.title: Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.
items.summary: The paper describes the development of a centrifugal microfluidic platform designed to simultaneously detect multiple respiratory pathogens, including influenza A and B, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV, in a point-of-care setting. The system integrates four independent reaction chambers preloaded with lyophilized reagents onto a single chip, paired with a portable analyzer that automates sample handling, isothermal amplification, and real-time fluorescence detection in a two-step workflow completed within fifteen minutes. The platform demonstrated very low limits of detection and showed no cross-reactivity against a panel of non-target pathogens. Clinical validation using a substantial set of positive patient samples yielded complete agreement with quantitative PCR for both positive and negative results. The authors conclude that the platform offers a practical combination of speed, simplified operation, minimal reagent consumption, and multiplexed detection suitable for decentralized diagnostic use.
items.citation: He P, Feng Y, Zhou X et al.. Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.. Biosensors & bioelectronics. 2026

items.title: Nanomaterials-enabled point-of-care diagnostics for pathogens.
items.summary: This review examines how nanomaterials can address key limitations of current point-of-care testing technologies for detecting pathogens, including insufficient sensitivity, specificity, and quantitative accuracy when dealing with low-abundance targets in complex clinical samples. The authors systematically survey the functional roles that representative nanomaterials play, encompassing optical signal output, catalytic signal amplification, target enrichment, and interfacial regulation. They then discuss how these nanomaterial properties enhance established diagnostic platforms such as lateral flow assays, biosensors, microfluidic systems, and isothermal nucleic acid amplification methods. Three major nanomaterial-assisted recognition mechanisms are identified—pathogen surface recognition, reactive oxygen species-mediated signal conversion, and nucleic acid recognition—and their applications across respiratory, urinary, and fecal specimens are described. The authors conclude that these advances collectively support the development of more sensitive, integrated, and field-deployable diagnostic systems for controlling infectious disease.
items.citation: Wu J, Wang D, Ye W et al.. Nanomaterials-enabled point-of-care diagnostics for pathogens.. Frontiers in medicine. 2026

items.title: Development of a rapid, sensitive and visual reverse transcription recombinase-aided amplification coupled with lateral flow dipstick assay for influenza B virus detection.
items.summary: The paper addressed the need for rapid, equipment-free detection of influenza B virus, which causes substantial seasonal disease burden but is poorly served by existing diagnostic methods that require complex instrumentation or lengthy turnaround times. The researchers developed a reverse transcription recombinase-aided amplification assay paired with a lateral flow dipstick readout, targeting the conserved non-structural gene of the virus. Optimal reaction conditions were established, and the assay was analytically validated for sensitivity and specificity against a panel of common respiratory pathogens including influenza A virus, SARS-CoV-2, parainfluenza virus, and adenovirus, with no cross-reactivity observed. Clinical evaluation showed complete concordance with standard PCR results. The authors conclude that the assay is a promising point-of-care and field surveillance tool due to its speed, sensitivity, specificity, and simplicity of operation without specialized equipment.
items.citation: Liu Y, Geng H, Wang Y et al.. Development of a rapid, sensitive and visual reverse transcription recombinase-aided amplification coupled with lateral flow dipstick assay for influenza B virus detection.. Frontiers in microbiology. 2026

items.title: Development and evaluation of a rapid duplex qPCR assay for Treponema pallidum using the GeneSoC microfluidic platform.
items.summary: This paper studied the development and evaluation of a rapid duplex quantitative PCR assay for detecting Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, to address the need for faster point-of-care molecular diagnostics. The researchers designed the assay on the GeneSoC microfluidic platform, targeting two genomic regions simultaneously, and tested it against DNA standards, a reference strain, and clinical specimens including lesion swabs and urine, with and without prior DNA extraction. The assay demonstrated good linearity and amplification efficiency across the tested concentration range and completed detection within fifteen minutes, substantially faster than the conventional thermal cycler comparator. It showed qualitative agreement with the comparator assay, no cross-reactivity with other pathogens, and was able to detect the pathogen in a specimen collected during the seronegative window period. The authors conclude that the microfluidic platform's rapid thermal cycling enables near-point-of-care syphilis detection without DNA extraction, though extraction may benefit specimens with very low pathogen loads.
items.citation: Kawahata T, Banno F, Hama M. Development and evaluation of a rapid duplex qPCR assay for Treponema pallidum using the GeneSoC microfluidic platform.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey
items.summary: This survey examines the intersection of foundation models and computational healthcare through a data-centric lens, focusing on how these AI systems can address longstanding challenges in clinical data acquisition, quality, and processing. The authors review a broad range of data-centric approaches spanning the full lifecycle of foundation models, from pre-training through inference, and how these approaches can improve healthcare workflows. The survey addresses critical concerns including data annotation, patient privacy, ethical considerations, and AI security, as well as alignment of these models with human values. The authors argue that the interactive, instruction-guided nature of foundation models represents a paradigm shift toward emphasizing data quality and scale rather than model architecture alone. The survey concludes with an optimistic outlook on the potential of foundation model-based analytics to enhance patient outcomes and streamline clinical workflows.
items.citation: Yunkun Zhang, Jin Gao, Zheling Tan et al.. Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey. ACM Computing Surveys. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical translation. The authors synthesize how approaches spanning genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics generate deep molecular insight into disease mechanisms, while deep learning architectures decode the resulting complex datasets to build predictive models. The review covers the application of this combined framework across the drug development pipeline, including target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound design, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Disease areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate the practical potential of these converging technologies. The authors also acknowledge persistent challenges, including harmonization of heterogeneous data streams, reproducibility concerns, and algorithmic bias, while arguing that overcoming these hurdles will define a new era of bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Detection to Disruption: A Comprehensive Review of Bacterial Biofilms and Therapeutic Advances
items.summary: This review examines bacterial biofilms, which are structured microbial communities encased in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance matrix that confers protection against antimicrobials and host immune defenses. The authors synthesize current knowledge on biofilm biology, covering the stages of biofilm development, matrix composition, and the physiological heterogeneity that emerges during maturation and underlies treatment failure. Multiple resistance mechanisms are discussed, including restricted antibiotic diffusion, enzymatic inactivation, efflux pump upregulation, persister cell formation, and horizontal gene transfer, as well as the clinical contexts in which biofilms are most problematic, such as cystic fibrosis, chronic wounds, osteomyelitis, and implant-associated infections. The review evaluates both conventional and emerging detection methods alongside therapeutic strategies that combine antibiotics with matrix-disrupting enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, bacteriophages, metabolic reactivators, and nanotechnology-based delivery platforms. The authors conclude that effective management of biofilm-associated infections requires integrated approaches that pair accurate detection with multifaceted therapies, and that advances in multi-omics and systems-level modeling will be critical for developing next-generation prevention and treatment strategies.
items.citation: Pranay Amruth Maroju, Angad S. Sidhu, Amogh R. Motaganahalli et al.. Detection to Disruption: A Comprehensive Review of Bacterial Biofilms and Therapeutic Advances. Antibiotics. 2026

items.title: Metal–Organic Framework Nanozymes: From Rational Design and Synthesis to Biomedical Applications
items.summary: This review examines metal-organic framework nanozymes, which are synthetic enzyme-mimicking materials whose catalytic activity is governed by the coordination of metal ions and organic ligands as well as their morphology and pore size. The authors identified a gap in the field, noting that a systematic framework connecting structural features to functional performance has been lacking. To address this, the review analytically covers how choices of metal ions, organic ligands, and particle morphology influence catalytic behavior, and it summarizes the advantages and limitations of various synthesis approaches. The review also presents case studies highlighting major biomedical applications of these nanozymes, with emphasis on the catalytic mechanisms underlying each application. The authors conclude by identifying key challenges facing the field and proposing directions for future research.
items.citation: Shundong Cai, Mengdie Li, S P Wang et al.. Metal–Organic Framework Nanozymes: From Rational Design and Synthesis to Biomedical Applications. Nano-Micro Letters. 2026
