items.title: Point prevalence assessments of five respiratory viruses in adults ≥ 50 years of age in Germany by multi-pathogen rapid antigen testing on June 1, 2024, and December 15, 2024.
items.summary: This study examined the circulation of five respiratory viruses among community-dwelling adults aged 50 and older in Germany using two single-day point prevalence assessments conducted in summer and winter of 2024. Participants performed multi-pathogen rapid antigen self-tests capable of detecting adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus, and reported associated symptoms, healthcare use, and work absence. The overall pathogen detection rate was low, with the majority of tests returning negative results, but adenovirus emerged as the most frequently detected pathogen on both assessment days, a finding that contrasts with its underrepresentation in routine surveillance. SARS-CoV-2 was associated with the greatest clinical and economic burden, most often prompting healthcare consultations and work absenteeism. The authors conclude that community-based point prevalence screening can uncover asymptomatic viral reservoirs and underreported circulation patterns, including frequent adenovirus co-detections that suggest a role as a co-infecting agent.
items.citation: Anggitakirana M, Nacov JA, Salmanton-García J et al.. Point prevalence assessments of five respiratory viruses in adults ≥ 50 years of age in Germany by multi-pathogen rapid antigen testing on June 1, 2024, and December 15, 2024.. Infection. 2026

items.title: 'No, it is a virus, your body will fight it.' The value of diagnostic testing for managing respiratory viruses in primary care: an observational study from a post-COVID pilot programme.
items.summary: This study examined the real-world impact of laboratory-based polymerase chain reaction testing for respiratory viruses, combined with rapid antigen testing for COVID-19, on patient management in a primary care setting during the pandemic. Using electronic medical records from a single urban general practice in New Zealand, researchers reviewed presentations over a period spanning before and after testing, analysing antibiotic prescribing, patient characteristics, follow-up communications, and presentation patterns. Over half of tested patients returned a positive result, yet antibiotics were prescribed at a notably high rate across all presentations, and patients who tested positive for a respiratory virus were actually more likely to receive antibiotics than those who tested negative. Test results were communicated to patients via text and email with some effectiveness, but gaps in result communication and inconsistent prescribing patterns were identified. The authors conclude that while advancing point-of-care technologies offering faster results may help address some limitations, broader environmental, clinical, and psychological factors also influence how test results are used in practice.
items.citation: Wesley-Smith L, Dowell A, Turner N et al.. 'No, it is a virus, your body will fight it.' The value of diagnostic testing for managing respiratory viruses in primary care: an observational study from a post-COVID pilot programme.. Journal of primary health care. 2026

items.title: A randomised, open-label clinical study on the efficacy of baloxavir marboxil and oseltamivir for post-exposure prevention of influenza in a hospital setting: a study protocol.
items.summary: This study protocol describes a clinical trial designed to evaluate the effectiveness of two antiviral drugs, baloxavir marboxil and oseltamivir, for post-exposure prophylaxis against influenza in hospital settings, where transmission risk is high and immediate isolation is not always feasible. The trial is a multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-controlled study enrolling close contacts of hospitalised patients with laboratory-confirmed influenza, who are randomised to receive baloxavir as a single dose, oseltamivir once daily for five days, or placebo. Participants will be monitored through respiratory sampling and symptom assessment at multiple time points, with the primary outcome being the five-day incidence of clinical influenza defined as laboratory-confirmed infection accompanied by fever and at least one respiratory symptom. Secondary outcomes include longer-term incidence of laboratory-confirmed influenza and the emergence of resistance-associated antiviral variants among those who become infected. The protocol establishes a framework for generating evidence on optimal prophylactic strategies to reduce hospital-acquired influenza transmission.
items.citation: Li X, Chu Z, Peng M et al.. A randomised, open-label clinical study on the efficacy of baloxavir marboxil and oseltamivir for post-exposure prevention of influenza in a hospital setting: a study protocol.. BMJ open. 2026

items.title: Respiratory multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests in New Zealand primary care: a mixed-methods pilot.
items.summary: This study piloted the integration of multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests into routine primary care settings in New Zealand to assess their feasibility, acceptability, and clinical utility for diagnosing acute respiratory infections. Using a mixed-methods design across seven primary care clinics during winter, the researchers combined electronic medical record audits with clinician and patient surveys, interviews, and focus groups to capture both quantitative outcomes and qualitative perspectives. Among a demographically diverse cohort of patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms, a meaningful proportion tested positive for at least one virus, and the tests were positively evaluated by virtually all clinicians and the large majority of patients. Clinicians reported that test results influenced antibiotic prescribing decisions and supported choices about secondary care referrals, while patients who tested positive were more likely to report intending to follow non-pharmaceutical measures to reduce transmission compared with those who tested negative. The authors conclude that these multi-viral tests were well-accepted and readily incorporated into practice, suggesting that routine use in primary care could improve management of common respiratory illnesses and encourage behaviour change to limit viral spread.
items.citation: Bibby S, Marsh S, Dowell A et al.. Respiratory multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests in New Zealand primary care: a mixed-methods pilot.. BJGP open. 2026

items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate article examines the longstanding question in exercise immunology of whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection. The paper pits opposing scholarly arguments against one another on several contested issues, including whether high-performance athletes are genuinely more infection-prone than the general population, whether exercise independently alters immunity beyond the effects of confounding factors such as sleep disruption, anxiety, nutritional deficits, and travel, and whether commonly used biomarkers and study designs are adequate to draw firm conclusions. There is broad agreement that regular moderate-intensity exercise of relatively short duration benefits immune defense, particularly in older adults and those with chronic disease, while arduous exercise typical of elite athletes and military personnel has long been thought to impair immunity. However, the article highlights a growing challenge to the view that exercise per se causes immunosuppression, noting that many lifestyle and environmental stressors unique to these populations activate the same immune pathways and may confound the evidence. Both sides agree that infection susceptibility is multifactorial, and the article calls for more rigorous empirical research to determine whether exercise itself is a causative factor in elevated infection risk among those who train at high intensities.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases to gather existing research on exercise immunology in individuals with spinal cord injury across patient, recreational, and athlete populations, while first outlining the relevant anatomical and physiological foundations of the immune and autonomic nervous systems. Spinal cord injury is associated with increased infection risk through multiple mechanisms, including reduced lymphocyte numbers and disrupted autonomic function that alters catecholamine concentrations, which in turn may directly suppress immune cells that express adrenergic receptors, with effects being especially pronounced in individuals with tetraplegia. However, the authors found that some immune responses to exercise, such as increased natural killer cell cytotoxicity and mucosal immunity changes in those with tetraplegia, appear to be independent of catecholamine responses and may resemble patterns seen in the able-bodied population. The review concludes that compensatory mechanisms such as sympathetic reflex activity, receptor hypersensitivity, and neuroendocrine adjustments may offset some disability-related immune deficits, and that rehabilitation and exercise can improve certain measures of immunity and autonomic function, suggesting exercise may be a valuable tool for maintaining health in this population.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria L. Goosey‐Tolfrey, Nicolette C. Bishop. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process
items.summary: This paper describes the development and goals of the Rome V diagnostic and classification framework for disorders of gut–brain interaction, conditions characterized by gastrointestinal symptoms arising from disturbances in motility, visceral sensitivity, mucosal function, gut microbiota, or central nervous system processing. The Rome V process involved a comprehensive review of evidence accumulated since the previous Rome IV criteria were published, with the aim of refining definitions, diagnostic algorithms, and therapeutic approaches. Key updates include incorporation of new knowledge on diet, the gut microenvironment, pharmacogenomics, biopsychosocial influences, and gender and cross-cultural factors, as well as a deliberate effort to eliminate imprecise or stigmatizing terminology. The framework also places greater emphasis on the patient illness experience and sociocultural context when approaching diagnosis and management.
items.citation: Douglas A. Drossman, L Chang, Jan Tack. Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process. Gastroenterology. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper examines graft-versus-host disease, a serious multi-systemic complication arising from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack host tissues, causing substantial morbidity and reduced physical capacity in long-term survivors. The authors reviewed the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease, with particular attention to its chronic form, alongside available evidence from both animal and human studies on the role of exercise as an adjunct therapy. Their review suggests that exercise training holds promise for improving physical fitness, potentially enhancing immune function, and reducing fatigue in affected patients. However, they conclude that the evidence base remains insufficient, calling for more rigorously designed randomized controlled trials focused specifically on this patient population.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: New approach methodologies for drug discovery
items.summary: This review examines the rise of new approach methodologies as alternatives to traditional animal-based drug discovery, which has historically suffered from high failure rates. The authors survey recent advances in stem cell-based systems, organoids, and computational modeling approaches, situating them within evolving regulatory frameworks from major health agencies. The review traces how these methodologies are being applied across the full drug-discovery continuum, from disease modeling and drug design through efficacy testing, and notably considers their potential as therapeutic interventions in their own right. Key biological, technical, and regulatory obstacles limiting widespread translational adoption are identified and discussed. The authors conclude by outlining future human-centric discovery pipelines and the broader translational and societal considerations necessary for responsible implementation of these approaches.
items.citation: Wenqiang Liu, Paul Pang, Catherine A. Wu et al.. New approach methodologies for drug discovery. Cell. 2026

items.title: Early Detection and Surveillance of the SARS-CoV-2 Variant BA.3.2 — Worldwide, November 2024–February 2026
items.summary: The paper examined the emergence and spread of SARS-CoV-2 variant BA.3.2, which was first identified in South Africa and subsequently detected across multiple countries including the United States. Researchers employed a multimodal genomic surveillance strategy incorporating traveler-based screening, clinical specimen analysis, airplane wastewater testing, and community wastewater surveillance to track the variant's introduction and dissemination. BA.3.2 carries a substantial number of substitutions and deletions in the spike protein relative to the antigens used in current vaccines, raising concern that existing immunity from prior infection or vaccination may offer reduced protection. Detection in the United States was captured through multiple surveillance streams, including travelers, clinical patients, and wastewater samples spanning numerous states, with the variant also reported in dozens of countries. The authors conclude that continued genomic surveillance is essential to monitor the evolution of BA.3.2 and assess its broader public health implications.
items.venue: MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.citation: Mila Shakya, Kevin C. Ma, Laura J. Hughes et al.. Early Detection and Surveillance of the SARS-CoV-2 Variant BA.3.2 — Worldwide, November 2024–February 2026. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over a five-year period, synthesizing the scientific evidence that has informed updated World Health Organization policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Key developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a frontline screening and triage tool, and the diversification of decentralised molecular diagnostics through low-complexity automated and manual nucleic acid amplification tests, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and approaches like sputum pooling to improve programmatic efficiency. Progress was also made in confirming tuberculosis bacteriologically in children and other sputum-scarce populations through expanded use of non-sputum specimens, while targeted next-generation sequencing has been endorsed for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level. Urine lipoarabinomannan assays improve diagnostic yield in people with HIV and advanced disease, and host blood transcriptomic signatures show promise for triage and prognosis, though no biomarker has yet met the criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical forms. The paper concludes that substantial gaps in diagnostic performance, implementation, and equity persist and identifies priority areas for continued development.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Predicted Preferences for Tuberculosis Point-of-Care Tests Among Tuberculosis-Affected Individuals in 5 High Burden Countries.
items.summary: This study examined how tuberculosis-affected individuals value point-of-care diagnostic tests relative to standard facility-based testing across five high-burden countries. Using discrete choice experiment data from over a thousand participants, the researchers simulated preferences for various tuberculosis testing scenarios. The findings indicate that point-of-care tests were strongly preferred by tuberculosis-affected persons, and this preference held even when point-of-care options offered modestly lower diagnostic accuracy than conventional tests. These results suggest that patient-centered factors beyond pure test performance play an important role in acceptance of tuberculosis diagnostics, with implications for how new tests should be developed and prioritized.
items.venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
items.citation: Nalugwa T, Shah KM, Marcelo D et al.. Predicted Preferences for Tuberculosis Point-of-Care Tests Among Tuberculosis-Affected Individuals in 5 High Burden Countries.. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2026

items.title: Clinical accuracy, performance, and usability of the Dragonfly point-of-care molecular diagnostic platform for mpox: a mixed-methods field evaluation in Uganda.
items.summary: This study evaluated the Dragonfly point-of-care molecular diagnostic platform for mpox detection in Uganda, a country among the most affected by the ongoing outbreak in east and central Africa. The researchers conducted a prospective diagnostic accuracy study across multiple health facilities in Kampala and Wakiso, enrolling individuals presenting with suspected mpox symptoms and testing cutaneous lesion swabs with Dragonfly—a dual-target platform detecting both orthopoxvirus and monkeypox virus—against confirmatory centralized quantitative PCR as the reference standard. Dragonfly demonstrated very high sensitivity and specificity for both targets, with results available in under forty minutes, performing consistently across a broad range of viral loads. Front-line users found the platform highly acceptable, particularly because it bypassed the need for centralized laboratory logistics, though they identified training and supply-chain requirements as considerations for routine implementation. The authors conclude that Dragonfly shows strong potential as a point-of-care diagnostic tool for mpox in resource-limited and high-burden settings, while calling for further research on cost-effectiveness, integration with existing diagnostics, and performance across different viral clades.
items.citation: Bakamutumaho B, Baker K, Cavuto ML et al.. Clinical accuracy, performance, and usability of the Dragonfly point-of-care molecular diagnostic platform for mpox: a mixed-methods field evaluation in Uganda.. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2026

items.title: To Bridge the Hepatitis B Diagnosis Gap in Africa, Innovation Must Go Beyond Digital.
items.summary: The abstract is too thin to summarize beyond its surface content: the paper argues that addressing the hepatitis B diagnosis gap in Africa requires nondigital approaches alongside digital innovations, and profiles a low-cost point-of-care diagnostic tool as an example of such complementary strategies in resource-limited settings.
items.citation: Muzaki S. To Bridge the Hepatitis B Diagnosis Gap in Africa, Innovation Must Go Beyond Digital.. Journal of medical Internet research. 2026

items.title: Better infectious disease diagnostics is crucial to tackling antimicrobial resistance.
items.citation: Abreu A, D'A Carvalho-Assef AP, Galas M et al.. Better infectious disease diagnostics is crucial to tackling antimicrobial resistance.. Lancet regional health. Americas. 2026

items.title: Utilizing rapid diagnostic tests in infectious disease surveillance and response in humanitarian emergencies.
items.summary: This paper examined the role of rapid diagnostic tests in managing infectious disease threats among populations affected by humanitarian emergencies, where access to conventional laboratory infrastructure is often severely limited. The authors conducted a landscape review of white and gray literature to assess the availability, technical characteristics, and operational strengths and weaknesses of existing rapid diagnostic tests for epidemic-prone infectious diseases in these settings, while also documenting tests under development. They found that low-cost, easy-to-use, and accurate rapid diagnostic tests are integral to infectious disease surveillance, outbreak detection, and response in humanitarian emergencies. The paper identifies barriers to wider adoption and discusses how complementary near point-of-care testing approaches could help address gaps. The authors conclude that field evaluations specifically conducted in humanitarian settings, pursuit of WHO pre-qualification for relevant tests, and country-level operational planning are key steps toward improving diagnostic capacity in these vulnerable contexts.

items.title: Smart wearable and implantable biosensors for continuous health monitoring: materials, biocompatibility, and AI integration
items.summary: This review examines smart wearable and implantable biosensors designed for continuous, real-time monitoring of biophysical and biochemical signals in the context of personalized and preventive healthcare. The paper surveys advances in flexible, stretchable, and biocompatible materials that enable long-term comfort and stable integration with the body, alongside multimodal and multi-analyte sensing approaches that improve measurement robustness. It also addresses how artificial intelligence is being integrated to enhance signal processing and generate predictive health insights. The review identifies persistent challenges including motion artifacts, energy autonomy, data privacy, and clinical interpretability that must be overcome for broader deployment. Overall, the paper synthesizes current progress across materials science, device architecture, and AI-assisted strategies to outline the state and trajectory of the field.

items.title: Gut microbiome and metabolic health: mechanisms and precision interventions
items.summary: This review examines the gut microbiome as a central regulator of metabolic health, exploring how microbial communities influence energy balance, insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and inter-organ communication through metabolites and signaling pathways. The authors synthesize mechanistic evidence spanning short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acid signaling, gut barrier integrity, immune modulation, and the microbiota-gut-brain-pancreas axis, drawing on findings from germ-free animal models, fecal microbiota transplantation studies, and strain-level interventions to argue that shifts in microbial ecology causally shape metabolic outcomes. Disease-associated microbial alterations across obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and metabolic syndrome are catalogued alongside an evaluation of therapeutic strategies including targeted probiotics, prebiotics, dietary interventions, and fecal microbiota transplantation. The review also addresses inter-individual variability in treatment responses and discusses how multi-omics technologies, microbial metabolic modeling, and machine learning are advancing precision microbiome medicine. To organize these findings, the authors propose a precision microbiome intervention pipeline and a conceptual Precision Microbiome Intervention Triangle intended to explain heterogeneity in responses to microbiome-targeted therapies and guide personalized metabolic interventions.
items.citation: Zhengrui Li, Sudeshna Samui, J S Liu et al.. Gut microbiome and metabolic health: mechanisms and precision interventions. Gut Microbes. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and translational medicine. The authors synthesize how approaches spanning genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics generate deep insight into disease mechanisms, while deep learning architectures decode these complex biological datasets to identify patterns and build predictive models. The review covers the application of this combined framework across the drug development pipeline, including target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound design, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Disease areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate how these technologies operate in practice. The authors conclude that while challenges such as data harmonization, reproducibility, and algorithmic bias remain, the convergence of multiomics and artificial intelligence opens new pathways for therapeutic innovation and more precise bench-to-clinic translation.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Functional chimeric mRNAs encode proteins in mammalian immunity
items.summary: This paper investigated whether mRNAs from different genes can undergo trans-splicing to generate chimeric transcripts that encode functional proteins during mammalian immune responses. Using a pipeline that combined long-read direct RNA sequencing with targeted and non-targeted validation in macrophages, the researchers identified chimeric transcripts produced through interchromosomal trans-splicing, with chromatin conformation capture revealing that inflammation promotes physical proximity between parent genes on different chromosomes. A key discovery was a chimeric mRNA fusing the pore-forming protein gasdermin D with a domain from Tmem106a, the expression of which is upregulated by inflammasome priming and whose encoded protein localizes to the plasma membrane. This chimeric protein interacts with canonical gasdermin D to accelerate and enhance pore formation and inflammatory cytokine release following inflammasome activation. In vivo experiments showed that this chimeric protein strikes a balance between host defence and immunopathology, with its loss protecting against lethal sepsis but impairing antibacterial defence, establishing that regulated chimeric mRNA formation is a biologically meaningful mechanism in inflammation and immunity.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals that inflammation can physically bring together chromosomal regions to generate chimeric mRNAs that produce functional proteins, challenging conventional views of how genes operate independently during immune responses. The finding that these chimeric transcripts encode physiologically relevant proteins suggests a previously unrecognized layer of gene regulation in mammalian immunity.
items.citation: Olivia Venezia, Harry Kane, Gang Du et al.. Functional chimeric mRNAs encode proteins in mammalian immunity. Nature. 2026

items.title: 3D epigenome of glial cell types in developing human cortex
items.summary: This study investigated the three-dimensional epigenomic landscape of glial cell types in the developing human cortex, focusing on four main populations — ventricular radial glia, outer radial glia, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and microglia — sampled from mid-gestational neocortex. The researchers integrated multiple genomic modalities, including gene expression, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional chromatin interaction data, to identify cell-type-specific candidate cis-regulatory elements and validate their function in transgenic mouse embryos. Using machine learning, the team prioritized schizophrenia risk variants residing within glial regulatory elements and confirmed in vivo that one specific risk allele disrupts a ventricular radial glia enhancer. The study also found that outer radial glia regulatory elements are enriched for human accelerated regions, and that a subset of these regions show activity differences compared to chimpanzee orthologues, with connections to genes involved in neuronal development. Together, these findings illuminate how cell-type-specific chromatin regulation in glial progenitors contributes to human cortical evolution and susceptibility to neuropsychiatric disorders.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it maps the three-dimensional epigenome of multiple glial cell types in the developing human cortex, revealing how non-coding genetic variants linked to neuropsychiatric disease and human-specific brain evolution are embedded within cell-type-specific regulatory architecture.
items.citation: Ian R. Jones, Li Wang, Michael Kosicki et al.. 3D epigenome of glial cell types in developing human cortex. Nature. 2026

items.title: Creating bottom-up RNA transfer vehicles from synthetic protein assemblies
items.summary: This paper investigated whether artificial intelligence-designed protein assemblies, which exist outside of natural evolutionary trajectories, could be engineered into functional RNA delivery vehicles. The researchers combined natural protein domains with synthetic protein assemblies generated by generative AI models to construct a large library of RNA transfer vehicles with diverse sizes and shapes distinct from naturally occurring viral capsids. These engineered vehicles substantially outperformed widely used RNA delivery systems in transfer efficiency, and their cell-type targeting could be programmed by incorporating computationally designed peptide binders. The vehicles were validated across numerous cellular models and demonstrated safe in vivo biodistribution in a mouse at near-single-cell resolution. As a proof of therapeutic application, the vehicles were used to deliver gene-editing cargo to correct the genetic defect underlying Duchenne muscular dystrophy in both patient-derived cells and a pig model.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because AI-designed synthetic protein assemblies can deliver RNA into cells more effectively than natural viruses, suggesting that bypassing evolutionary constraints allows for superior gene delivery vehicles.

items.title: Late-life semaglutide treatment slows ageing and extends lifespan in female mice
items.summary: This study investigated whether the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide, a drug used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity, could influence the ageing process and lifespan when administered late in life. Aged female mice were treated with semaglutide for several months, and its effects were compared directly against matched calorie restriction in a longitudinal study. Treatment with semaglutide improved physiological function, attenuated hallmarks of ageing, and modulated nutrient-sensing pathways and conserved genetic regulators of ageing, with continued treatment ultimately extending lifespan. Semaglutide recapitulated many benefits of calorie restriction but also produced superior outcomes in exploratory drive, spatial memory, and glucose control compared to calorie restriction alone. The authors conclude that GLP-1 receptor activation acts as a calorie restriction mimetic and propose this mechanism as a framework to explain the broad pleiotropic benefits of GLP-1 medicines beyond simple reductions in food intake.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it suggests that semaglutide, a drug already in widespread clinical use, can slow biological ageing and extend lifespan when given late in life, at least in female mice. The findings are notable because the treatment improved physiological function and reduced hallmarks of ageing, raising the possibility that existing medications could be repurposed to target the ageing process itself.
items.citation: Yufan Feng, Marine Barthez, Yifei Wang et al.. Late-life semaglutide treatment slows ageing and extends lifespan in female mice. Nature. 2026

items.title: Robust inference and correlates from genetic associations with personality
items.summary: This paper investigated the genetic basis of the Big Five personality traits — extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness to experience — by conducting large-scale genome-wide association studies across numerous cohorts spanning over a million participants with European-like and African-like ancestry. The researchers performed meta-analyses of standard and within-family genetic association studies, and applied polygenic index, genetic correlation, and Mendelian randomization analyses to assess robustness, confounding, and downstream relevance of personality-associated genetic variants. They identified over a thousand lead genetic variants associated with personality, the majority of which were novel, and found that common genetic variants explain a modest but meaningful proportion of variance in each trait. Genetic associations were broadly consistent across geography, age, measurement instrument, and reporter type, and within-family analyses indicated that, unlike many other behavioural traits, personality genetics are minimally confounded by shared family environment. The authors conclude that the genetic architecture of personality is robustly generalizable and has widespread, potentially causal relevance to a range of important life behaviours and outcomes.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it demonstrates that the genetic basis of personality traits is broadly applicable across populations, largely free from confounding factors, and meaningfully connected to a wide range of human outcomes and experiences.

items.title: Exploring baryon semileptonic decays through polarization and entanglement
items.summary: This paper investigates hyperon semileptonic decays as an alternative means of precisely determining the CKM matrix element governing strange-to-up quark transitions, motivated by existing tensions between measurements from kaon and tau decays that may signal physics beyond the Standard Model. Previous experiments studying hyperon semileptonic decays lacked sufficient kinematic information to probe the relevant form factors effectively, so the researchers exploited the polarization and quantum entanglement of Lambda-antiLambda pairs produced at the J/ψ resonance to extract detailed decay information. Using this approach, they measured axial-vector and weak-magnetism couplings in the Lambda hyperon semileptonic decay, and obtained the first determinations of the absolute branching fraction and weak-electricity coupling for this channel. Combining their experimental results with recent lattice QCD calculations yielded a model-independent determination of the CKM element consistent with unitarity of the CKM matrix. The method substantially enhances single-event sensitivity and is broadly applicable to other baryon semileptonic decays, establishing a framework for a systematic research programme capable of achieving precision rivaling that of kaon decay measurements.
items.why_notable: By leveraging polarization and quantum entanglement measurements in baryon semileptonic decay, this work achieves greatly enhanced single-event sensitivity that, combined with theoretical calculations, yields a precise determination of a key quark-mixing matrix element. This provides an independent test of the standard model, making it notable for probing fundamental symmetries and potential physics beyond current theory.
items.citation: M. Ablikim, M. N. Achasov, P. Adlarson et al.. Exploring baryon semileptonic decays through polarization and entanglement. Nature. 2026

items.title: Explainable deep learning improves human mental models of self-driving cars
items.summary: This paper investigated whether explainable artificial intelligence techniques could improve human understanding of self-driving car behavior in real-world conditions. The researchers developed the Concept-Wrapper Network, a method that grounds the reasoning of deep neural network-based planners in human-interpretable concepts while maintaining driving performance, and deployed it on an actual self-driving vehicle rather than in simulation. They found that the explanations generated by this approach enhanced the mental models of human drivers, enabling them to more accurately predict vehicle behavior, especially in unexpected or surprising scenarios. The work demonstrates that explainable deep learning can be both comprehensible and practically useful in realistic autonomous driving deployments, not merely in controlled or simulated settings. The authors propose that their approach could extend to other safety-critical autonomous systems and different neural network architectures, offering a validated pathway toward greater transparency and safety in autonomous agents.

items.title: The nutritional value of invertebrate aquatic foods
items.summary: This paper investigated the nutritional contributions of aquatic invertebrates to human diets, a food group whose dietary importance is often underappreciated. The researchers quantified the global nutrient supply provided by current aquatic invertebrate production and modeled the estimated nutrient content across tens of thousands of macroinvertebrate species. They found that these organisms are exceptionally rich in a wide range of micronutrients and fatty acids, with current production capable of meeting the annual requirements of billions of people for nutrients such as vitamin B12, selenium, copper, omega-3 fatty acids, iodine, and zinc. Nutrient profiles varied according to taxonomic group, environmental conditions, life-history traits, and consumption patterns. The authors argue that better integration of aquatic invertebrates into dietary guidelines, food policy, and sustainability assessments could yield significant public health and nutritional benefits globally.

items.title: Intracellular complement factor H protects neurons during CNS inflammation
items.summary: This study investigated why certain neurons are more resilient than others to degeneration during central nervous system inflammation, using multiple sclerosis as the disease context and retinal ganglion cells as a model system. Through single-nucleus RNA sequencing of retinal tissue from donors with multiple sclerosis and healthy controls, the researchers discovered that expression of complement factor H strongly correlated with neuronal survival. Experimentally, they found that complement factor H is induced in neurons under inflammatory and oxidative stress conditions, where it functions intracellularly at the endoplasmic reticulum to limit reactive oxygen species accumulation and lipid peroxidation, thereby protecting against ferroptosis. Critically, this protective function depended on a specific protein domain and operated independently of complement factor H's known secreted form and canonical complement pathway activity, revealing a non-canonical intracellular role for this protein. These findings identify complement factor H as a key mediator of neuronal resilience across the central nervous system in both mice and humans, with potential implications for neuroprotective therapies in multiple sclerosis.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it identifies a complement protein operating inside neurons—rather than in the bloodstream—as a key protector of neuronal resilience during central nervous system inflammation, with findings shown to be relevant in both mice and humans.

items.title: Structure and operating principles of a monkeypox virus replisome
items.summary: This study investigated how the monkeypox virus assembles a functional replisome to replicate its genome, focusing on the interaction between the viral polymerase and the helicase-primase complex. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the researchers determined structures of DNA-bound replisomes containing the three-subunit polymerase holoenzyme together with the hexameric helicase-primase. They found that replisome assembly triggers large-scale conformational changes in the helicase-primase, causing two of its primase domains to interact directly with specific polymerase subunits. Biochemical and single-molecule experiments demonstrated that this conformational rearrangement simultaneously activates helicase activity and enhances primase activity, resolving how the previously autoinhibited helicase becomes activated. These findings reveal the structural and mechanistic basis by which monkeypox virus coordinates helicase and polymerase functions during DNA replication, with implications for understanding a medically important class of pathogens.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals the molecular architecture and mechanistic details of how the monkeypox virus copying machinery assembles and activates, showing that dramatic structural rearrangements in a key enzyme drive its activation through specific interactions with the polymerase complex. items.title: Blood cells replace the immune cells of the ageing human brain
items.summary: Research examined whether microglia — the brain's resident immune cells, established at birth — truly persist for life without outside contribution, as previously thought. Using mutational analysis and cell lineage tracing approaches, the work investigated the origins of immune cells found in the aging human brain. The findings demonstrate that bone marrow-derived circulating blood cells colonize the brain during aging, replacing the original microglia population. This reveals a previously unrecognized dynamic interaction between the peripheral immune system and the brain that challenges the long-held view of microglial self-sufficiency throughout life.

items.title: Early Detection and Surveillance of the SARS-CoV-2 Variant BA.3.2 — Worldwide, November 2024–February 2026
items.summary: This paper examined the emergence and early spread of the SARS-CoV-2 variant BA.3.2, which was first identified in South Africa in late 2024. The authors employed a multimodal genomic surveillance approach, drawing on traveler-based genomic surveillance, clinical specimen testing, airplane wastewater analysis, and community wastewater monitoring to track the variant's international and domestic spread. BA.3.2 carries a large number of substitutions and deletions in its spike protein relative to the antigens used in current COVID-19 vaccines, raising concern that it may reduce protection conferred by prior infection or vaccination. Surveillance detected the variant across dozens of countries, and within the United States it was found in travelers, clinical patients, and wastewater samples spanning a substantial number of states. The authors conclude that continued genomic surveillance is essential to monitor the ongoing evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and assess the public health implications of variants like BA.3.2.
items.venue: MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.citation: Mila Shakya, Kevin C. Ma, Laura J. Hughes et al.. Early Detection and Surveillance of the SARS-CoV-2 Variant BA.3.2 — Worldwide, November 2024–February 2026. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 2026

items.title: Metagenomic Sequencing for Wastewater-Based Surveillance: Modeling and Experimental Approaches for Determining Limit of Detection
items.summary: This paper investigated the use of metagenomic next-generation sequencing as a tool for wastewater-based surveillance, focusing on understanding its limit of detection and related performance characteristics that have limited its broader adoption compared to PCR-based methods. The researchers developed a computational model to estimate operational detection limits for various sequencing approaches within a simplified local wastewater system based on a military installation, and they conducted two complementary types of experiments using a bacterial organism spiked either into wastewater samples in the laboratory or directly into a real-world wastewater system at a source location. The findings demonstrate that metagenomic sequencing detection performance depends substantially on the choice of sequencing method and the data analysis pipeline employed. The study also found that laboratory-spiked experiments do not fully replicate the conditions encountered in system-spiked experiments, highlighting the importance of site-specific method characterization. The authors conclude that because wastewater systems differ in configuration, background microbial communities, and sequencing inhibitors, implementations of metagenomic sequencing for surveillance should be validated individually at each site.
items.citation: Xiao A, Besse K, Connors D et al.. Metagenomic Sequencing for Wastewater-Based Surveillance: Modeling and Experimental Approaches for Determining Limit of Detection. 2026

items.title: Wastewater Surveillance for Early Warning of Infectious Disease Outbreaks: A Systematic Review of Evidence and Implications for One Health Surveillance.
items.summary: This systematic review examined the role of wastewater surveillance in providing early warning of infectious disease outbreaks and its alignment with One Health principles, which integrate human, animal, and environmental health monitoring. The authors searched multiple major databases and screened hundreds of studies, ultimately synthesizing findings from those meeting strict inclusion criteria. The review found a consistent positive association between pathogen detection in wastewater and clinical case counts in communities, with respiratory and gastrointestinal pathogens predominating and seasonal patterns observed across identified organisms. Targeted sampling in socially vulnerable areas and appropriate collection frequency were identified as particularly valuable for early outbreak detection. However, the review also revealed that few studies have explicitly operationalized a One Health framework, and the authors call for standardized surveillance methods and stronger integration of human, animal, and environmental monitoring systems in future wastewater surveillance programmes.
items.citation: Panigrahi S, Pattnaik M, Pradhan R et al.. Wastewater Surveillance for Early Warning of Infectious Disease Outbreaks: A Systematic Review of Evidence and Implications for One Health Surveillance.. Pathogens (Basel, Switzerland). 2026

items.title: International Airport Wastewater as a Sentinel Site for Genomic Surveillance of Human Viruses and Bacteriophages.
items.summary: This study investigated whether international airport wastewater could serve as a sentinel site for detecting human-associated viruses and bacteriophages, addressing a gap in metagenomic surveillance research in South America. Researchers collected untreated wastewater samples from a major Brazilian airport over a period spanning late 2021 to early 2023 and analyzed them using hybrid-capture target-enriched next-generation sequencing to characterize the virome. The analysis identified hundreds of viral and bacteriophage-associated taxa, including numerous human-associated viruses spanning multiple viral families, with norovirus detected in every sample and SARS-CoV-2 co-detected alongside dengue virus in one collection. Bacteriophage profiling revealed dozens of host-associated phage groups, with those linked to Streptococcus predominating, offering indirect signatures of the microbial communities carried by the traveling population. The authors conclude that airport wastewater effectively captures diverse pathogen signals reflective of population mobility and has strong potential as an environmental genomic surveillance tool for early warning of emerging and circulating pathogens.
items.citation: Carvalho APA, Almada MS, Leal CD et al.. International Airport Wastewater as a Sentinel Site for Genomic Surveillance of Human Viruses and Bacteriophages.. Microorganisms. 2026

items.title: Clade-specific multiplex digital PCR assay for monkeypox virus detection in spike-in wastewater samples.
items.summary: This paper developed and validated a multiplex digital PCR assay for detecting and quantifying monkeypox virus in wastewater samples. The study focused on distinguishing between the major clades and subclades of the virus, which is epidemiologically important because these clades differ in transmissibility and mortality. The researchers validated a four-plex digital PCR approach using spike-in wastewater samples, evaluating its linearity, sensitivity, and specificity. The assay demonstrated strong analytical performance across all targets, with limits of detection in the low single-digit copies per reaction range, and successfully differentiated between viral clades. The authors propose this tool as valuable for wastewater-based epidemiological surveillance, offering a population-level monitoring approach that is independent of individual clinical testing.
items.citation: Pitton M, Gan C, Schmidhalter P et al.. Clade-specific multiplex digital PCR assay for monkeypox virus detection in spike-in wastewater samples.. Access microbiology. 2026

items.title: Inferring variant-specific effective reproduction numbers from combined case and sequencing data
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating the transmission rates of co-circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants by jointly analyzing confirmed case counts and genetic sequencing data. The authors extended existing methods for inferring effective reproduction numbers to simultaneously estimate variant-specific effective reproduction numbers and variant frequencies across states in the United States over a period spanning early 2021 to early 2022. Their approach allows structured relationships between reproduction numbers to be inferred across time series, enabling estimation of fixed variant-specific growth advantages that remain consistent across geographic locations. Applying this framework to variants of concern and variants of interest, they demonstrate that using case data alongside sequence proportions captures richer epidemiological dynamics than sequencing data alone. The method yields estimates of consistent growth advantages for specific variants across different locations, providing a more complete picture of variant transmission than frequency-based approaches.
items.citation: Marlin D Figgins, Trevor Bedford. Inferring variant-specific effective reproduction numbers from combined case and sequencing data. eLife. 2026

items.title: Mobile Genetic Elements as Central Drivers of Antimicrobial Resistance: Molecular Mechanisms, Evolutionary Ecology, One Health Implications and Control Strategies
items.summary: This review examines the central role of mobile genetic elements in driving the global spread of antimicrobial resistance across bacterial species and ecosystems. The authors synthesized current knowledge by critically evaluating recent genomic, epidemiological, and ecological studies alongside case studies of clinically significant resistance outbreaks, covering diverse elements including plasmids, integrons, transposons, insertion sequences, integrative and conjugative elements, and prophages. The review finds that these elements act as hubs for the capture, recombination, and stabilization of antibiotic resistance genes, enabling the emergence of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant pathogens. Ecological pressures such as antibiotics, heavy metals, and biocides are identified as drivers that influence mobile genetic element dynamics, while One Health transmission pathways connect resistance dissemination across human, animal, and environmental compartments. The authors argue that linking these molecular insights to applied interventions — including genomic surveillance, mobile genetic element-targeted inhibitors, phage therapy, and CRISPR-based strategies — is essential for developing effective responses to the antimicrobial resistance crisis.
items.citation: Hemayet Hossain, Md. Hasan Ali, Tanvir Ahmad et al.. Mobile Genetic Elements as Central Drivers of Antimicrobial Resistance: Molecular Mechanisms, Evolutionary Ecology, One Health Implications and Control Strategies. Antibiotics. 2026

items.title: The WHO priority list of antibiotic-resistant bacteria: challenges and opportunities for next-generation antimicrobial development
items.summary: This narrative review examines the global threat posed by antimicrobial resistance, focusing on the bacterial pathogens designated as priorities by the World Health Organization to guide drug development and research investment. The authors synthesize current understanding of the molecular mechanisms by which these pathogens evade existing antibiotics, encompassing reduced membrane permeability, efflux pump overexpression, enzymatic inactivation, target modification, biofilm formation, and horizontal gene transfer. The review critically evaluates why conventional antibiotic discovery pipelines have largely failed to keep pace with resistance, and assesses a range of emerging therapeutic strategies—including artificial intelligence-assisted drug discovery, phage therapy, antimicrobial peptides, CRISPR-based approaches, and natural product-derived compounds—with attention to their translational challenges, toxicity, dosing, and regulatory hurdles. The authors also emphasize the importance of antimicrobial stewardship, global surveillance, and a One Health framework that integrates human, animal, and environmental health sectors. The overall conclusion is that confronting priority resistant pathogens will require multidisciplinary approaches that connect molecular biology, pharmacology, clinical translation, and public health.
items.citation: Emad M. Abdallah, Abdulrahman Mohammed Alhudhaibi, Mahmoud M. Dahab et al.. The WHO priority list of antibiotic-resistant bacteria: challenges and opportunities for next-generation antimicrobial development. Frontiers in Pharmacology. 2026

items.title: Disinfection in wastewater treatment: From conventional to emerging technologies
items.summary: This review paper examines the full landscape of wastewater disinfection technologies, from established methods to emerging alternatives, in the context of growing challenges facing treatment plants. The authors critically synthesize how conventional approaches such as chlorination, ultraviolet radiation, and ozonation work and where they fall short, particularly regarding antibiotic-resistant bacteria and genes, complex wastewater matrices, and the formation of harmful disinfection byproducts. Special focus is placed on advanced oxidation processes and hybrid systems, which can simultaneously inactivate microorganisms and remove micropollutants. The review also addresses the integration of real-time monitoring and artificial intelligence tools for predicting disinfection performance and optimizing chemical use. The authors conclude that combining advanced treatment technologies with intelligent monitoring systems will be essential for achieving microbial safety, byproduct control, energy efficiency, and economic viability under increasingly stringent regulatory requirements for wastewater reuse.
items.citation: Mariana Costa, Daniel Terrón, Cristiano Leal et al.. Disinfection in wastewater treatment: From conventional to emerging technologies. Journal of Water Process Engineering. 2026

items.title: Postbiotics and phage synergy in precision oral microbiome engineering: systems biology strategies targeting Streptococcus mutans in dental caries
items.summary: This review examines the potential of postbiotics as precision tools for managing dental caries by targeting the oral microbiome and virome, with particular focus on the pathogenic bacterium Streptococcus mutans. The authors synthesize current knowledge on how non-viable microbial products and metabolic derivatives—including organic acids, bacteriocins, exopolysaccharides, and structural components from inactivated probiotic cells—can reduce biofilm acidogenicity, disrupt bacterial communication, weaken extracellular matrix integrity, and modulate mucosal immune responses while preserving commensal microbial balance. The review further explores synergistic strategies combining postbiotics with bacteriophage-based therapies, nanoformulations, and bioadhesive delivery systems to improve site-specific efficacy against cariogenic biofilms. The authors highlight how multi-omics technologies, systems biology modeling, and artificial intelligence-driven diagnostics could enable personalized interventions tailored to individual oral microbial signatures, and note that postbiotic modulation of viral-bacterial interactions may help curb antimicrobial resistance dissemination. The review concludes by identifying key translational obstacles—including formulation stability, safety evaluation, regulatory pathways, and comprehensive virome profiling—that must be addressed before these approaches can reach clinical application.
items.citation: Guhanraj Radhamanalan. Postbiotics and phage synergy in precision oral microbiome engineering: systems biology strategies targeting Streptococcus mutans in dental caries. Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences. 2026

items.title: Two extremely irradiated volatile-rich sub-Neptunes with companions in the TOI-426 and TOI-1839 systems: Insights into arrival and survival near the lower edge of the Neptunian desert
items.summary: This study confirmed two highly irradiated sub-Neptune planets situated near the lower boundary of the Neptunian desert, a region of orbital parameter space where planets are rarely found, using space-based photometry and a large set of ground-based radial velocity measurements. The researchers characterized both planets' bulk properties and modeled stellar activity contamination, also detecting additional companions in each system, including a long-period giant planet in one system and a second transiting sub-Neptune in the other. Despite receiving extraordinarily high levels of stellar irradiation, the densities of all three transiting planets require substantial volatile content, and atmospheric escape modeling strongly favors water-dominated rather than hydrogen/helium envelopes, pointing to a steam-world composition that can survive on billion-year timescales. A population-level analysis revealed a striking statistical excess of outer giant companions specifically among low-mass planets residing in the predicted tidal survival band near the desert's lower edge, compared to those outside it. These findings together suggest that the lower boundary of the Neptunian desert is shaped not solely by photoevaporation of primordial envelopes but also significantly by high-eccentricity tidal migration driven by outer giant companions.
items.citation: A. Castro-González, O. Barragán, D. J. Armstrong et al.. Two extremely irradiated volatile-rich sub-Neptunes with companions in the TOI-426 and TOI-1839 systems: Insights into arrival and survival near the lower edge of the Neptunian desert. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Ion abundances in the plasma tail of 3I/ATLAS show that it is N2-rich
items.summary: This paper studied the chemical composition of the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, by analyzing ion emissions in its plasma tail. Using integral-field unit spectroscopy with the WHT/WEAVE-LIFU instrument on two dates following perihelion, the researchers detected multiple ionic species — including N2+, CO+, CO2+, H2O+, and CH+ — concentrated in an anti-solar tail. By applying fluorescence factors to the observed ion abundances, they derived abundance ratios among these species and used the N2+/CO+ ratio to establish a lower limit on the N2/CO ratio in the comet. The results indicate that 3I/ATLAS is significantly enriched in nitrogen gas relative to Solar System comets, a characteristic interpreted as evidence for cold formation conditions in its home planetary system. The overall ion abundance pattern is also consistent with a general enrichment in hypervolatiles, and only a marginal spatial variation — a decrease in CH+ with distance along the tail — was detected.
items.citation: Lea Ferellec, Cyrielle Opitom, Colin Snodgrass. Ion abundances in the plasma tail of 3I/ATLAS show that it is N2-rich. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Propagation Model for SSC attacks: Why SBOM (tools) don't tell the whole truth
items.summary: This paper investigates the limitations of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) tools in securing software supply chains, arguing that these tools fail to capture how vulnerabilities propagate through an entire chain. The authors developed a four-stage propagation model designed to assess how security weaknesses spread from structural exposure through to taint path analysis. They empirically evaluated four open-source SBOM tools against this model using three software projects and the Log4j vulnerability as a case study. Their findings reveal that current SBOM tools systematically address only the first two stages of the model, covering structural exposure and vulnerability class presence, while lacking the capabilities needed for code reachability analysis and taint path analysis. The authors conclude that centering software supply chain security research on propagation effects is essential to prevent localized cyber risks from escalating into broader systemic risks.
items.citation: Ljubica Grgic, Lazar Maksimovic, Pavel Laskov. Propagation Model for SSC attacks: Why SBOM (tools) don't tell the whole truth. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Coincidence-based spectral engineering for spectral matching in cascaded downconversion
items.summary: This paper investigates the generation of three-photon entangled states through cascaded spontaneous parametric downconversion, where a key challenge is achieving spectral compatibility between successive nonlinear optical stages. The authors demonstrate that by filtering the herald photon in coincidence with detection, one can conditionally reshape the spectrum of its entangled partner, tailoring it to match the acceptance bandwidth of the second nonlinear stage without modifying the sources themselves. They employed an electro-optically gated spectrometer to directly measure the conditional spectra governing the cascaded process, enabling quantitative predictions of the enhancement in conversion probability per detected herald. Photon-triplet measurements were then used to verify these predictions, confirming improved performance at fixed heralding rates. The work establishes coincidence-based spectral engineering as a practical method for overcoming spectral incompatibility in cascaded downconversion, especially in scenarios constrained by detector saturation or mismatched source bandwidths.
items.citation: Mohammed Charafi, Alexandre Z. Leger, Samridhi Gambhir et al.. Coincidence-based spectral engineering for spectral matching in cascaded downconversion. arXiv. 2026

items.title: When LLM Decompilers Recompile More and Preserve Less
items.summary: This paper investigates whether current evaluation metrics for large language model-based decompilers—specifically recompilability and re-executability—adequately capture decompilation quality. The authors demonstrate that these metrics can be misleading: a decompiled function may successfully build and pass all shipped tests while diverging from the original binary's behavior on other inputs, and security-relevant crashes from known vulnerabilities may silently disappear from the recompiled code. To address this, they introduce Decompile-Diverge, a behavioral comparison oracle that automatically synthesizes test drivers, grows fuzzing corpora from the reference binary, and checks whether the decompiled code produces matching behavior across those inputs. Applying this framework to established benchmarks, real library functions, and vulnerability-grounded test cases, they find that functions passing all shipped tests still exhibit behavioral divergence at meaningful rates, and that LLM refinement can simultaneously improve build rates while reducing behavioral fidelity and suppressing crash-triggering behavior in vulnerable functions. Source-level analysis traces these divergences to LLM-introduced fields, types, callees, and guards that silently resolve the ambiguities that traditional decompilers leave as visible placeholders.
items.citation: Chang Liu, Edward Raff, Kristopher Micinski. When LLM Decompilers Recompile More and Preserve Less. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Dust Substructures and Line Perturbations driven by a Forming Planet in J16120
items.summary: This study investigated the protoplanetary disc around a young star for evidence of active planet formation, building on prior hints from multiple observational wavelengths. Using high-resolution millimeter and submillimeter observations from ALMA, the researchers mapped dust continuum emission and molecular line emission to characterize both the disc structure and gas dynamics. Analysis of the dust continuum revealed an inner disc and two dust rings, with the overall morphology better described by an eccentric disc model than a symmetric one. Examination of gas kinematics uncovered a localized increase in velocity dispersion, kink-like features, a shift between sub- and super-Keplerian velocities, and an arc-like residual structure, all spatially coincident with a previously identified circumplanetary disc candidate. These kinematic signatures are consistent with predictions from planet–disc interaction simulations and, together with the dust morphology, provide compelling evidence that a planet is actively forming within the disc gap.
items.citation: Anibal Sierra, Andrés F. Izquierdo, Paola Pinilla et al.. Dust Substructures and Line Perturbations driven by a Forming Planet in J16120. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Research progress on nucleic acid amplification–based detection technologies for phytopathogenic fungi
items.summary: This review paper examines the threat posed by phytopathogenic fungi to global agriculture, noting that fungal pathogens account for the vast majority of plant disease infections and are responsible for substantial annual crop yield losses worldwide. The authors surveyed the principles and recent advances of nucleic acid amplification-based detection technologies as applied to identifying these pathogens. The technologies reviewed span thermal cycling approaches such as conventional PCR, real-time quantitative PCR, and droplet digital PCR, as well as isothermal amplification methods including loop-mediated isothermal amplification and recombinase polymerase amplification. The review also covers CRISPR/Cas-assisted detection systems that couple isothermal amplification with CRISPR diagnostics, highlighting their potential for field-deployable, low-instrumentation use. The authors evaluate the strengths and limitations of each approach, arguing that integrated molecular detection workflows can support early diagnosis and precision management of phytopathogenic fungal diseases.
items.citation: Baoyu Wang, Mei Liu, Hui Wang et al.. Research progress on nucleic acid amplification–based detection technologies for phytopathogenic fungi. Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Rapid and Sensitive Detection of <i>Schistosoma mansoni</i> in the Intermediate Snail Hosts Using Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Diagnostics.
items.summary: The study addressed the need for improved detection of *Schistosoma mansoni* infection in its intermediate snail hosts, which is critical for schistosomiasis control but poorly served by conventional parasitological methods. Researchers developed a loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay targeting the mitochondrial NADH dehydrogenase subunit 1 gene of *S. mansoni*, optimizing it for a simple, single-temperature reaction, and evaluated it against microscopy, conventional PCR, and real-time PCR using both laboratory-infected snails and field-collected samples from two African countries. The new assay achieved perfect specificity and high sensitivity in laboratory conditions, outperforming microscopy and matching real-time PCR performance. In field surveys, it detected a higher proportion of infected snails than conventional PCR, while microscopy failed to identify any positive individuals, highlighting its superior sensitivity in real-world settings. The authors conclude that this assay represents a sensitive, specific, and practically deployable tool for routine surveillance of snail infection and early detection of changes in schistosomiasis transmission.
items.citation: Li HM, Qin ZQ, Lv S et al.. Rapid and Sensitive Detection of <i>Schistosoma mansoni</i> in the Intermediate Snail Hosts Using Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Diagnostics.. Tropical medicine and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: Development of a Novel <i>Pseudoperonospora cubensis</i>-Specific LAMP Assay for Rapid Field Detection and Surveillance of Cucurbit Downy Mildew.
items.citation: Waliullah S, Anwar MT, Ali E. Development of a Novel <i>Pseudoperonospora cubensis</i>-Specific LAMP Assay for Rapid Field Detection and Surveillance of Cucurbit Downy Mildew.. Journal of fungi (Basel, Switzerland). 2026

items.title: Dual readout RT-LAMP for rapid on-site dengue virus detection and serotyping.
items.summary: This study addressed the need for rapid, field-deployable dengue virus diagnostics by developing four serotype-specific reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification assays. Primer design was guided by analysis of thousands of whole-genome sequences spanning diverse geographical regions, with degenerate bases incorporated to maximize coverage of global viral genetic diversity while limiting the number of distinct oligonucleotides required. The assays operate at constant temperature, eliminating the need for thermal cyclers, and feature a dual readout system allowing both real-time fluorescence monitoring and simple visual colorimetric interpretation without instruments. Clinical evaluation using PCR-confirmed patient samples covering serotypes one through three showed strong detection rates, with complete detection achieved for one serotype, and no cross-reactivity was observed between serotypes. Results are obtained within forty to sixty minutes, making these assays well suited for point-of-care deployment in resource-limited, dengue-endemic settings.
items.citation: Brambilla R, Rockwood N, Michel J et al.. Dual readout RT-LAMP for rapid on-site dengue virus detection and serotyping.. Microbiology spectrum. 2026

items.title: Broad-Temperature Polymerase in Nucleic Acid Amplification-Based Diagnostics: From Thermal Precision to Dynamic Conditions.
items.summary: This paper investigated nucleic acid amplification methods that can function across a wide range of temperatures, addressing the limitations of conventional approaches that require precise thermal control. The researchers developed a LAMP-based amplification system using a Bst polymerase with strong strand displacement activity and broad thermostability, enabling DNA synthesis across a temperature range from below typical LAMP conditions to temperatures approaching those used in PCR. They demonstrated that amplification could be initiated at both high and low starting temperatures and sustained even under dynamically changing temperature profiles rather than fixed conditions. The system was validated for detecting SARS-CoV-2 and mycobacterial genomic DNA, confirming its diagnostic utility. The authors propose this broad-temperature amplification platform as a promising tool for point-of-care and field diagnostics where maintaining strict thermal regulation is impractical.
items.citation: Hamidizadeh M, Bier FF. Broad-Temperature Polymerase in Nucleic Acid Amplification-Based Diagnostics: From Thermal Precision to Dynamic Conditions.. ACS sensors. 2026
